Along ℓ there is a periodically repeating pattern: squares appear alternately above and below ℓ; the bottom side of each upper square is on ℓ, and the upper right corner of each upper square is connected to a short line segment slanting toward the upper right; the top side of each lower square is on ℓ, and the lower left corner of each lower square is connected to a short line segment slanting toward the lower left. Reasoning: Check the four types of rigid motions one by one. 1. Rotation about some point on ℓ: there exists a 180° rotation that maps an upper square and its upper-right slanted line segment to the adjacent lower square and its lower-left slanted line segment, and because the pattern repeats infinitely and periodically, the whole remains unchanged, so this type is feasible. 2. Translation in a direction parallel to ℓ: translating by one complete period length will move each upper square to the next upper square and each lower square to the next lower square, and the whole remains unchanged, so this type is feasible. 3. Reflection about ℓ: an upper square would be reflected to the lower side at the same horizontal position, but the lower squares in the figure are staggered; the positions and directions of the slanted line segments also do not match, so it is not feasible. 4. Reflection about some line perpendicular to ℓ: the upper side remains on the upper side and the lower side remains on the lower side, but the left-right direction of the slanted line segments would be reversed, for example the upper-right slanted line of an upper square would become an upper-left slanted line, and there is no such correspondence in the figure, so it is not feasible. Therefore, among the four types, there are 2 types of non-identity rigid motions that can transform the figure into itself.

method.method_draft: Use a direct visual symmetry check. First read the image as a horizontal line \(\ell\) with an infinite periodic pattern: squares above \(\ell\) repeat at equal spacing, squares below \(\ell\) repeat at equal spacing and are offset between the upper squares; each upper square has a short diagonal segment from its upper-right corner slanting up-right, and each lower square has a short diagonal segment from its lower-left corner slanting down-left. From the text, test the four listed transformation types, excluding identity. A horizontal translation by one full repeat length maps each upper square to the next upper square and each lower square to the next lower square, so it works. A 180-degree rotation about an appropriate point on \(\ell\) between an upper square and its adjacent lower square maps an upper square and its up-right segment to the corresponding lower square and down-left segment, and repeats through the infinite pattern, so it works. Reflection across \(\ell\) fails because it would put an upper square directly below its same horizontal position and would put the diagonal on the wrong corner/direction. Reflection across a line perpendicular to \(\ell\) fails because it would keep upper squares above the line but reverse their diagonal segments to upper-left slants, which do not occur. Therefore exactly 2 of the four kinds work.

method.method_draft: Model the pattern with coordinates. Let \(\ell\) be the \(x\)-axis. From the image, assign a side length \(s\), a repeat period \(T\), and an offset \(a\) so that upper motifs occur as squares above the axis, for example on intervals \([kT,kT+s]\), with a short segment attached at the upper-right corner; lower motifs occur on intervals \([kT+a,kT+a+s]\) below the axis, with a short segment attached at the lower-left corner. The text asks which of the four classes of isometries has at least one non-identity member preserving the entire infinite set. Translation \((x,y)\mapsto(x+T,y)\) sends every upper motif to the next upper motif and every lower motif to the next lower motif, so translation counts. A half-turn about the point \(((a+s)/2,0)\) on \(\ell\), and its periodically shifted equivalents, sends the interval of an upper square to the interval of the adjacent lower square and sends the upper-right diagonal to the lower-left diagonal, so rotation counts. Reflection in the \(x\)-axis sends the upper-right diagonal to a lower-right diagonal and does not match the observed lower-left diagonals or horizontal offset, so it does not count. Reflection in any vertical line \(x=c\) would turn an upper-right diagonal into an upper-left diagonal while keeping it above \(\ell\), but no upper-left diagonal motifs appear in the image, so no perpendicular reflection works. The count is 2.
